entries.title: Will you buy any of the new Kindle 2026 e-readers?
entries.summary: Would you pay more for 13th-generation Kindle e-readers, such as the Kindle, Kindle Paperwhite, and Kindle Colorsoft? The post Will you buy any of the new Kindle 2026 e-readers? first appeared on Good e-Reader.
entries.content:
Amazon surprised many people in the industry and customers worldwide when it announced a bevy of new Kindle e-readers. Instead of having just one model in each category, they now offer a couple. Some use the typical plastic, while others have an aluminum backing that makes them feel more premium. Some are available to order now, such as the base Kindle, Kindle Paperwhite, and the Paperwhite Signature Edition, while the two new Colorsoft units won’t ship until the end of October; the same goes for the new Kindle Clip and the cases with physical page-turn buttons.

Paperwhite

Amazon has just announced two new Kindle Paperwhite e-readers. Now thinner and lighter, with a 7-inch flush-front display, up to 12 weeks of battery life, adjustable warm light, and waterproofing. The Signature Edition adds aluminum, adaptive front lighting, 32GB of storage, and ad-free reading. Both will be available for purchase on October 28th 2026, with pre-orders happening right now.

The all-new Kindle Paperwhite is thinner and lighter than the previous lineup, waterproof, with an adjustable warm light for comfortable reading at any hour, and up to 12 weeks of battery life on a single charge. The Paperwhite display uses an oxide-thin film transistor backplane and is the largest Kindle Paperwhite display with the highest contrast ratio—delivering deep blacks and crisp text, and images that pop off the screen.

Both Kindle models have a resolution of 300 PPI. VoiceView screen reader, available over Bluetooth audio. : Supports 2.4 GHz and 5.0 GHz networks with support for WEP, WPA, WPA2 and WPA3 security using password authentication. The dimensions are 26.8 mm x 174.7 mm x 6.8 mm

Available with 16GB of storage in Graphite starting at $199.99. Signature Edition with 32GB of storage is available in Graphite and Seaglass Green at $249.99.

Kindle Colorsoft 2026

Amazon just announced the Kindle Colorsoft e-reader, with a base model for $289 and a Signature Edition for $319 with an aluminum back plate. It has 32GB of storage, an auto-adjusting front light, and double-tap page-turning. Both are available for purchase on October 28th 2026.

The new Kindle Colorsoft delivers paper-like color that’s easy on the eyes without the harsh glare of a tablet. Whether you’re scrolling through colorful covers in your library or flipping through a travel guide, comic, or graphic novel, the display makes color reading feel natural. To achieve paper-like color, our Kindle Colorsoft display includes a light guide with nitride LEDs to enhance color and increase brightness, all without washing out details. It uses an oxide backplane with custom waveforms for fast performance and higher contrast in both color and black-and-white content.

The latest Kindle Colorsoft has a completely redesigned display, using the reverse printing technology they applied across the lineup for edge-to-edge color. The light guide contains micro-deflectors that minimize stray light and improve uniformity, and an ultra-thin optical coating in the display stack improves clarity.

The Colorsoft Signature Edition adds aluminum housing, 32GB of storage, an auto-adjusting front light, double-tap to

turn pages, and dock charging via pogo pins. Both models have a resolution of 300 PPI for black-and-white text and 150 PPI for Color. It supports the VoiceView screen reader, available over Bluetooth audio.

Kindle

The all-new 6-inch Kindle is the most pocket-sized Kindle they have ever made. With 16GB of storage, up to six weeks of battery life, and 30% faster book opening than the previous release, it is lighter and features a new seamless flush-front design. This required rethinking how the display, front light, and touch layers are assembled and bonded. They are also introducing edge-to-edge color across the entire family. The housing is made from recycled materials with a 100% recycled cobalt battery. Starting at $149.99 and available in Ube and Graphite.

This 6-inch Kindle is also available for the first time with an aluminum back—same pocket-sized form factor, same flush-front display, but with a premium feel you notice the moment you pick it up, and that younger readers are used to from reading on other devices. The housing is crafted from 80% recycled aluminum with a matte finish. Kindle in aluminum has 32GB of storage and is available in two colors, Alpine Sky Aluminum and Seaglass Green Aluminum.

Both Kindle models have 300 PPI resolution and support VoiceView screen reader, available over Bluetooth audio. Supports 2.4 GHz and 5.0 GHz networks with support for WEP, WPA, WPA2, and WPA3 security using password authentication.

Wrap up

The new Kindle e-readers have increased in price since the previous generation’s price increase a month ago. It is hard to justify upgrading from the 12th generation to the 13th generation. However, the screen tech seems a bit refined. Aluminum gives them a slightly better design, and there are plenty of new covers.

Will you buy any of the new Kindle models, or will you instead buy the Kindle Clip, a wireless Bluetooth page-turn product designed by Amazon?

entries.title: Amazon Kindle Click is not shipping anytime soon
entries.summary: The Amazon Kindle Click release date has been pushed back for new orders, from November to March next year. The post Amazon Kindle Click is not shipping anytime soon first appeared on Good e-Reader.
entries.content:
The Amazon Kindle Click is a new wireless Bluetooth page-turner, the first of its kind that Amazon developed itself. The company told Good e-Reader that, due to demand, the product won’t ship to people who ordered it on day 1 until November 11th 2026, and many orders have been pushed back to March 2027. The Amazon Kindle case with page-turn buttons has also been pushed back into next year.

Kindle Click costs $34.99 USD and $47 CAD and is available on all major Amazon websites. It has two big buttons: one to turn pages forward and the other to turn back. Kindle Click comes in one color: white, and the buttons are grey. It comes with a lanyard to attach to your wrist, with a small hole for the attachment, but it is optional. A small battery powers it, and you charge it with a USB cable.

I don’t think Amazon anticipated how popular the Kindle Click would be and didn’t keep an adequate stockpile in the countries where it’s marketed, such as Canada, the UK, Japan, and the United States.

entries.title: Why Your E-Reader Sells a Different Bookstore in Every Country
entries.summary: It is tempting to read regional restrictions as the retailer being difficult The post Why Your E-Reader Sells a Different Bookstore in Every Country first appeared on Good e-Reader.
entries.content:
The same Kindle, the same account, the same title. Cross a border and the buy button disappears. Here is what is actually happening behind that message.

The message every traveling reader eventually sees

Anyone who has owned a Kindle or a Kobo for more than a year has probably met it: “Due to copyright restrictions, the Kindle title you are trying to purchase is not available in your country.” On Kobo the wording is softer, the title simply fails to appear in search, or shows up with no price attached. On Libby, the library card that worked at home stops returning results the moment the app decides you are somewhere else.

None of this is a bug. It is the visible edge of a licensing system that predates e-readers by decades, and that the devices themselves inherited without much modification. Understanding it explains a lot of otherwise baffling behavior, from the regional catalog mismatch between amazon.com and amazon.co.uk to why a Tolino bought in Germany behaves nothing like the same hardware sold in Italy.

Books are licensed by territory, not by language

When an author signs with a publisher, the contract rarely grants “world rights.” English-language rights are commonly split three ways: North America, the United Kingdom and Commonwealth, and everything else. A different publisher can hold each slice. A Canadian imprint might have the print edition but not the ebook. A UK house might have the ebook but only for markets outside the US.

Retailers then have to enforce these boundaries at the point of sale. Amazon, Kobo, Apple Books and Google Play all receive metadata from publishers that lists the countries in which a given edition may be sold. If your account is registered in a country that is not on that list, the edition is hidden or blocked. The territorial rights model is why two customers sitting side by side on the same Wi-Fi network can see different prices, different covers, or different availability for a single ISBN.

Self-published titles tend to be the exception. An author uploading directly through KDP or Kobo Writing Life usually keeps world rights and ticks every territory, which is why indie catalogs feel more consistent across borders than traditional ones.

How the store decides where you are

This is where e-readers differ from, say, a streaming app on a phone. A dedicated reading device makes very few network requests, and most of them are to a single vendor. So the store leans less on your current IP address and more on account metadata.

On Kindle, the deciding factor is the “Country/Region” setting under Manage Your Content and Devices, which Amazon ties to a billing address and a payment method. Kobo binds the account to the country selected at signup and to the local partner store (Indigo in Canada, Rakuten in Japan, Fnac in France, Walmart in the US). Libby and OverDrive check library card eligibility, which in most public systems requires proof of residency in a specific municipality or county.

IP location still plays a part, though. Amazon compares the country of your connection against the country on file, and enough mismatches will prompt a request to update the address. Kobo’s web store redirects to a regional domain based on IP before you ever sign in. The broader mechanics of how services fingerprint a visitor’s location, and what changes when that signal is masked, are laid out in Gizmodo’s explainer on how location-based content restrictions work, which is useful background for anyone trying to work out whether an ebook problem is an account issue or a network one.

What the regulators actually decided

Readers in Europe often assume this kind of restriction was outlawed years ago. The rule they are thinking of is the EU geo-blocking regulation, which banned retailers from redirecting or refusing customers based on their member state. But the text carves out copyright-protected digital content by name. Ebooks, along with music, software and video, sit outside the ban on differential access. The retailer must let you see the site, but it does not have to sell you the book. The full text of Regulation (EU) 2018/302 spells this out in Article 4, and a scheduled review in 2020 left the exemption in place.

The reasoning offered at the time was that removing the exemption would collapse territorial licensing and, in countries with fixed book price laws such as France and Germany, undermine the pricing regime that keeps independent bookshops alive. Whether that logic holds for digital files is a debate the industry has yet to settle.

The practical fallout on the device

A few consequences follow directly from all this, and they explain some of the stranger support threads on any e-reader forum.

Purchased books travel with you. Rights are checked at the time of sale, not at the time of reading. A title bought while the account was set to the US remains readable after moving to Spain, even if it is no longer purchasable there. The library is not retroactively pruned.

Changing your account country is a real change, not a cosmetic one. On Kindle it can wipe your Kindle Unlimited subscription, alter what is eligible for Prime Reading, and reset the store to a currency that may not match your card. Amazon also requires a local payment method for some regions. On Kobo, switching countries can orphan a partner-store account entirely.

Library apps are the strictest of all. Because Libby and OverDrive licenses are negotiated per library system, not per publisher, there is no account setting to change. Eligibility is whatever the card allows, and many systems now verify address at renewal.

Sideloading bypasses the store but not the DRM. An EPUB bought from a regional store still carries Adobe or Kobo DRM tied to the account that bought it. A DRM-free EPUB, which is what most small presses and technical publishers sell, moves between devices and countries with no restriction whatsoever. This is the strongest argument for buying DRM-free where it is available.

What to check before assuming the catalog is broken

When a title refuses to appear or to sell, the order of diagnosis is fairly consistent. Confirm the account country in the store’s settings, since a stale address from a previous move is the single most common cause. Then check whether the edition exists at all in your region by searching the retailer’s local domain from a browser rather than from the device, which has a much smaller search interface. Then look at the publisher listed on the product page; if it is an imprint you associate with a different market, the edition is probably not licensed where you are.

Only after those three steps does the connection itself become a suspect. E-readers cache location decisions aggressively, and a device that made its first store request from a hotel abroad may keep serving that region until it is deregistered and set up again.

The catalog is a map of contracts, not a map of the world

It is tempting to read regional restrictions as the retailer being difficult. In most cases the retailer would rather sell the book. What the device is showing you is the shape of a rights agreement negotiated between an author, an agent and a handful of publishers, often years before the ebook edition existed. The hardware simply renders it. Knowing that will not make the buy button reappear, but it does make the next “not available in your country” message a great deal easier to interpret.

Markus lives in San Francisco, California and is the video game and audio expert on Good e-Reader! He has a huge interest in new e-readers and tablets, and gaming.

entries.title: E INK is making color chaging clothes
entries.summary: E INK has partnered with a Japanese fashion house for a series of color e-paper dresses that will be sold to the public in 2027. The post E INK is making color chaging clothes first appeared on Good e-Reader.
entries.content:
E INK has just entered into a creative relationship with ANREALAGE, the avant-garde Japanese fashion house. Through the collaboration, ANREALAGE incorporated E Ink Prism 3 into six color-changing dresses in its 2027 “SKIN” collection, presented during Paris Fashion Week, which began on September 29th.

The collaboration brings together traditional textile craftsmanship and modern material technology. Known for challenging conventional ideas about form, perception, and materials, Morinaga uses E Ink Prism to push conventionally static fashion to a new dimension—one in which movement is expressed not only through the shape of a garment, but also through its changing appearance.

For the ANREALAGE collection, each color-changing dress features approximately 1,000 to 2,000 individual E Ink Prism pieces. Arranged in a scale-like pattern, the elements work together to create additional outfits out of a singular garment. As a result, the technology provides a sustainable way to multiply the creative possibilities of an individual piece.

What is E INK Prism?

E Ink Prism is a dynamic material technology that brings programmable color and pattern surfaces of all shapes and sizes – from color-changing cars, automotive interiors, fashion accessories, handbags, and more. Unlike traditional light-emitting displays, E Ink technology is reflective, relying on ambient light to make colors visible. Its bistable properties allow an image to remain in place without continuously consuming power. Energy is only required when the display changes.

“ANREALAGE has a long history of combining craftsmanship, technology, and imagination in ways that challenge how we see everyday materials,” said Naoki Sumita, President of E Ink Japan. “That ethos closely aligns with E Ink’s vision of transforming traditionally static surfaces into dynamic, expressive experiences. This collaboration demonstrates how E Ink Prism can unlock new possibilities for personalization, movement, and visual expression.”

entries.title: Audible Launches Character Guide, Interactive Stories, and Visual Explore
entries.summary: Audible is announcing 3 new AI-powered features designed to let listeners see who's speaking, talk to characters, and explore a story's world. The post Audible Launches Character Guide, Interactive Stories, and Visual Explore first appeared on Good e-Reader.
entries.content:
Audible is announcing 3 new AI-powered features designed to let listeners see who’s speaking, talk to characters, and explore a story’s world. All three features are rolling out in a limited beta for U.S. and UK Audible customers and will evolve based on customer and creator feedback.

Audible is introducing three new features that deepen listeners’ connections to their favorite stories: Character Guide, which shows who is speaking and who’s who in a complex cast; Interactive Stories, which let listeners talk with characters in real time; and Visual Explorer, which surfaces maps and imagery that reveal the world behind the story. All three are built in close collaboration with creators, using AI to enhance the listening experience.

“These new features invite listeners into a story in ways that simply weren’t possible before, marking the latest step in our nearly 30-year journey to push audio storytelling forward,” says Audible’s Chief Content Officer, Rachel Ghiazza. “We’re excited to build on these while working hand in hand with creators, because we know that more time spent with stories benefits everyone who helps bring them to life.”

“Audible continues to be the premier destination for audio storytelling. We are always innovating new ways to deepen customers’ engagement as they listen,” says Andy Tsao, Chief Product and Analytics Officer at Audible. “In this case, AI is allowing us to create new interactive experiences that today’s listeners, especially younger audiences, are craving.”

entries.title: Amazon releases their first Bluetooth Page-Turn – Click
entries.summary: The Kindle Click is a Bluetooth Page-Turner compatible with all new Kindle devices, as well as any Kindle model from 2024 or later. The post Amazon releases their first Bluetooth Page-Turn – Click first appeared on Good e-Reader.
entries.content:
Amazon has just released a new compact Bluetooth remote for page turning—ideal for reading under the covers, on a treadmill, or on a tray table during a flight. It is called Kindle Click and is compatible with all new Kindle devices, as well as any Kindle model from 2024 or later.

Kindle Click costs $34.99 and is available on all major Amazon websites. It has two big buttons: one to turn pages forward and the other to turn back. Kindle Click comes in one color: white, and the buttons are grey. It comes with a lanyard to attach to your wrist, with a small hole for the attachment, but it is optional.

The good thing about the Click is that, like the Kobo Remote, it doesn’t need an attachment on the e-reader’s screen; it is completely wireless. It is unclear whether it has a battery or charges via USB-C.

Introducing All-New Amazon Kindle Click — Bluetooth Page-Turn Remote for Kindle Devices...

  • Turn pages without reaching for your Kindle – Compatible with all Kindle devices (2024 Release and Onward). Pairs over Bluetooth so you turn pages forward and back while your Kindle stays in place.
  • Brightness and sleep control at your fingertips – Dedicated side buttons let you adjust the screen brightness without opening a menu. Press both to put your Kindle to sleep without reaching for it.
  • Rechargeable battery that lasts for weeks – Read for weeks on a single charge, then recharge over USB-C. (USB-C cable and adapter sold separately.)

entries.summary: Amazon just released a new series of Kindle covers. One of the most compelling is a new one with physical page-turn buttons. The post Amazon releases new Kindle Covers, including one with page-turn buttons first appeared on Good e-Reader.
entries.content:
Amazon just released a new series of Kindle covers. One of the most compelling is a new one with physical page-turn buttons. The magnetic cover helps keep it slim, attaches to the Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition and Kindle Colorsoft Signature Edition via Pogo pins, and costs $79.99.

The base Kindle also has a number of new cases available in a knit fabric, plant-based leather, and pebbled premium leather covers

that wrap fully around the device for a seamless finish, color-matched across the lineup. For devices with aluminum housing, slim magnetic-attach covers are also available. These cost $39.99.

Amazon said in a statement that “Reading is an immersive, joyous experience, and we’ve watched Kindle fans engineer their own reading setups for years—propping devices on pillows, rigging phone stands as makeshift docks, and hunting for the easiest possible page turn. We designed a system for the people who take their reading experience as seriously as we do.”
